slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
'Why did that work?' Students redo the 2.5 bisector construction, then try a small radius on purpose and watch it fail.

  • I can prove the perpendicular-bisector construction works by SSS and then SAS.
  • I can state when the construction circles fail to cross twice and why that breaks the proof.

slides.title: Optional extension
slides.html:
Optional extension: the perpendicular bisector construction, proved in three stages.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Circles of the same radius at A and B cross at P and Q, on opposite sides of AB. Let M be the point where PQ meets AB.Define M before using it.
N is the midpoint of segment AB. The Ruler Postulate guarantees every segment has a midpoint, so N exists before we draw anything.The Ruler Postulate guarantees every segment has a midpoint.
Turn the whole picture halfway around N. This half-turn moves A to where B was, and B to where A was.Half-turn: a rotation of 180 degrees about a point (Unit 3).
A half-turn keeps every distance the same. So the circle around A lands on the circle around B, and the circle around B lands on the circle around A.Rotations preserve distance (Unit 3). The two circles have equal radii.
The half-turn also flips the two sides of line AB. P is on one side and Q is on the other. So P lands on Q, and Q lands on P.P and Q are the only two points where the circles cross.
A half-turn sends each point straight through N to the other side. The point lands the same distance from N as it started.Definition of a half-turn.
P lands on Q. So N is exactly halfway from P to Q. N is the midpoint of PQ.Use the last two rows together.
N is on segment PQ and on segment AB. So PQ crosses AB at N. That crossing point is M, so M is N. M is between A and B and between P and Q, and ray PM is ray PQ.Two different lines cross in at most one point.
M is between A and B, and also between P and Q. So ray PM is ray PQ.Shown by the half-turn rows just above.
AP = BP, AQ = BQ, PQ = PQ, so triangle APQ ≅ triangle BPQ.SSS.
So angle APM = angle BPM.CPCTC, and PM lies along PQ.
AP = BP and PM = PM, so triangle APM ≅ triangle BPM.SAS.
AM = BM, and angles AMP and BMP are equal.CPCTC.
Those two angles add to 180, so each is 90. PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB.Linear pair.

geo.title: Optional extension
geo.prompt: Optional extension: the perpendicular bisector construction, proved in three stages.

steps.step: Circles of the same radius at A and B cross at P and Q, on opposite sides of AB. Let M be the point where PQ meets AB.
steps.reason: Define M before using it.

steps.step: N is the midpoint of segment AB. The Ruler Postulate guarantees every segment has a midpoint, so N exists before we draw anything.
steps.reason: The Ruler Postulate guarantees every segment has a midpoint.

steps.step: Turn the whole picture halfway around N. This half-turn moves A to where B was, and B to where A was.
steps.reason: Half-turn: a rotation of 180 degrees about a point (Unit 3).

steps.step: A half-turn keeps every distance the same. So the circle around A lands on the circle around B, and the circle around B lands on the circle around A.
steps.reason: Rotations preserve distance (Unit 3). The two circles have equal radii.

steps.step: The half-turn also flips the two sides of line AB. P is on one side and Q is on the other. So P lands on Q, and Q lands on P.
steps.reason: P and Q are the only two points where the circles cross.

steps.step: A half-turn sends each point straight through N to the other side. The point lands the same distance from N as it started.
steps.reason: Definition of a half-turn.

steps.step: P lands on Q. So N is exactly halfway from P to Q. N is the midpoint of PQ.
steps.reason: Use the last two rows together.

steps.step: N is on segment PQ and on segment AB. So PQ crosses AB at N. That crossing point is M, so M is N. M is between A and B and between P and Q, and ray PM is ray PQ.
steps.reason: Two different lines cross in at most one point.

steps.step: M is between A and B, and also between P and Q. So ray PM is ray PQ.
steps.reason: Shown by the half-turn rows just above.

steps.step: AP = BP, AQ = BQ, PQ = PQ, so triangle APQ ≅ triangle BPQ.
steps.reason: SSS.

steps.step: So angle APM = angle BPM.
steps.reason: CPCTC, and PM lies along PQ.

steps.step: AP = BP and PM = PM, so triangle APM ≅ triangle BPM.
steps.reason: SAS.

steps.step: AM = BM, and angles AMP and BMP are equal.
steps.reason: CPCTC.

steps.step: Those two angles add to 180, so each is 90. PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps.reason: Linear pair.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan uses M without defining it.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A proof that uses M without saying what M is, is not finished. Define M as the point where PQ meets AB. The radius must be more than half of AB, not equal to it.

geo.correction: A proof that uses M without saying what M is, is not finished. Define M as the point where PQ meets AB. The radius must be more than half of AB, not equal to it.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
AB = 10 and the radius is 4. Do the circles cross twice?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. 4 + 4 = 8, which is less than 10.

Reveal second check

The two circles can't reach each other.

geo.title: Practice 1
geo.prompt: AB = 10 and the radius is 4. Do the circles cross twice?
geo.check: The two circles can't reach each other.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Why isn't radius 5 enough?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The circles only touch once, at the midpoint, so there aren't two points to draw a line through.

Reveal second check

The radius has to be more than half of AB.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
In the angle bisector proof, what is the third SSS fact?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

OX = OX.

Reveal second check

The shared side is in both triangles.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
Which congruence test proves that the angle bisector construction works?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

SSS: vertex to each arc mark (equal), each mark to the crossing point (equal), and the shared segment from the vertex to the crossing point.

Reveal second check
